new_statements.rule_in_words: In the priests' traditional reading pronunciation of Classical Mandaic (and equally in the vernacular), the word accent is culminative and never further back than the antepenult: disyllables are stressed on the penult; in words of three or more syllables the penult is stressed if it is long (long vowel or closed), otherwise the antepenult - the East-Syriac/Latin-type quantity-sensitive rule. Native words are not normally stressed on the ultima.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.137 speaks of a 'secondary accent' that always remains on a restored full vowel in an originally pretonic open syllable (émar 'he said', never amar; getal with a full vowel 'in the secondarily stressed open syllable'); no general rhythmic secondary-stress rule is given in the snippets seen.
new_statements.exceptions: p.139: Sheikh Abdullah (Macuch's priestly informant) stressed the ultima in some 'original Mandaic words, in which other Mandaeans usually stress the penult'; Persian loanwords 'can keep the principal stress on the ultima, esp. when the penult is short' (deráxt 'tree', pašimán 'sorry') but a long penult is regularly stressed (nówkar); p.265: longer ethpa. verb forms prefer penult stress, shorter pa. forms antepenult; p.148: a short open stressed penult gets its following consonant doubled so that the stressed syllable is heavy.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of citation/reading forms; stated jointly for the traditional (liturgical reading of Classical texts) and colloquial (Neo-Mandaic) pronunciations recorded by Macuch in Ahwaz 1953. Enclitics (l-, b- + suffix) are written and pronounced as one word with the verb (Nöldeke 1875:13 'ein Wort mit einem Hauptton'; Macuch §§81, 238).
new_statements.identity_note: Macuch 1965 §90 states one accent rule for 'the traditional and colloquial pronunciations of Mandaic': 'traditional' = the priests' (tarmidi) reading pronunciation of the Classical Mandaic literary language (clas1253, informant chiefly Sheikh Abdullah Khaffagi of Ahwaz), 'colloquial' = the Neo-Mandaic vernacular of Khuzistan (Glottolog nucl1706). Classical Mandaic is a liturgical/literary language with no native speakers, so any stress statement necessarily concerns the reading tradition; Malone 1997 (p.156) treats the stress of Classical Mandaic as historically spoken only as a reconstruction (either MM-like or word-final like early Syriac). Macuch p.139 notes Sh. Abdullah idiosyncratically stressed the ultima of some native words 'in which other Mandaeans usually stress the penult'. Häberl 2019 (saved) describes Neo-Mandaic of Khorramshahr (nucl1706), not clas1253, with a differently formulated weight rule (closed tense-vowel ultima stressed, else heavy penult, else antepenult).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is culminative and falls on the penult or the antepenult. The antepenult is stressed only in words of three or more syllables whose penult is short (light); otherwise (penult long by nature or by position, or word of fewer than three syllables) the penult is stressed. A stressed syllable must as a rule be heavy (long by nature or position), so a short open penult that receives stress gets its consonant doubled (p.148). Stated for the traditional and colloquial (modern) pronunciations of Mandaic; the rule is explicitly compared to Syriac.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as a rule. §90 (p.137) uses 'secondary accent' only historically: when an unstressed short vowel after the stressed syllable was apocopated, the accent moved to the original antepenult ('which became a secondary penult'), and 'the secondary accent always remains: émar (never amar)'; p.265 notes the longer ethpa. verb forms prefer penult stress while shorter pa. forms are supposed to have antepenult stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p.139 (§95-96): final (ultima) stress occurs 'in Sh. Abdullah's pronunciation of original Mandaic words, in which other Mandaeans usually stress the penult'; original Persian loanwords 'can keep the principal stress on the ultima, esp. when the penult is short, cf. deráxt "tree", pašimán "sorry"'; 'When the penult is long, it is regularly stressed, cf. nówkar'. p.138 (§92): a short vowel before the principal accent is syncopated and the accent then passes to the preceding syllable (gitlat getlat, gumla gómlā, malka málkā).
new_statements.identity_note: Macuch's §90 rule is stated for 'the traditional and colloquial pronunciations of Mandaic', i.e. the priestly reading tradition of the classical texts and the modern colloquial (Ahvaz/Khorramshahr) pronunciation together; it is what the catalog uses for Classical Mandaic. The p.139 ultima-stress remarks concern one informant's (Sheikh Abdullah's) pronunciation and Persian loanwords.

sources.citation: Kaufman, Stephen A. 1997. Aramaic; and Jastrow, Otto. 1997. The Neo-Aramaic Languages. In R. Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Kaufman: in later classical Aramaic 'stress was generally on the final syllable.. though the modern dialects (and some reading traditions) show a strong tendency toward penultimate stress' (no Mandaic-specific statement). Jastrow: Neo-Mandaic has penultimate stress (gévra 'man', hā́zya 'she sees') like most Eastern Neo-Aramaic. Neither addresses Classical Mandaic.
